title: Degree bounds the span of an integral curve, with the minimal-degree equality case
statement:
Let $k$ be algebraically closed [def-weil-field], $r\ge2$, and let $Y\subset\mathbf P^{r-1}_k$ be an integral closed subscheme of dimension one [def-pc-integral-scheme, def-weil-closed-immersion]. Let $\nu:\widetilde Y\to Y$ be its normalization [def-sc-normalization], and set $e=\deg(\nu^*\mathcal O_Y(1))$ [def-pc-degree-line-bundle, def-pc-projective-space-twist]. Write $V=H^0(\mathbf P^{r-1}_k,\mathcal O(1))\cong k^r$ and
$$s=\dim_k\operatorname{im}\bigl(V\longrightarrow H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y(1))\bigr).$$
Then $e$ is a positive integer, $2\le s\le e+1$, and $s=e+1$ holds if and only if $Y$ is a rational normal curve in its own linear span: $Y\cong\mathbf P^1_k$, with its given embedding in that span the morphism of the complete linear system $|\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1}(e)|$. In particular, if $Y$ is not such a curve, then $s\le e$.

proof.text: Put $C=\widetilde Y$ and $L=\nu^*\mathcal O_Y(1)$. An integral curve is connected, reduced and generically reduced, and has just one reduced irreducible component. Apply [lem-sfb-projective-curve-normalization-section-defect] to $X=Y$: its structural assertions give a smooth proper connected curve $C$ and the positive integer $e=\deg L$. Only these structural assertions are used, not its eventual-in-$m$ estimates. By [lem-sc-normalization-properties](a), $\nu$ is surjective and birational. By [lem-sc-proper-dim-one-projective], $C$ is projective, since its dimension is one.

source.place: Tags 0BXR (normalization), 0B5X (ample line bundles on curves); structural specialization of the cited projective-curve node

proof.text: Pullback $H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y(1))\to H^0(C,L)$ is injective: birationality identifies the generic fibres, so a section whose pullback is zero has zero generic germ, hence is zero by [lem-sc-invertible-module-generic-stalk](3), with $X=Y$ and $U=Y$. Let $U$ be the image of $V$ in $H^0(C,L)$; then $\dim U=s$. The restricted homogeneous coordinates generate $\mathcal O_Y(1)$, and their pullbacks generate $L$, since on the chart $x_i\ne0$ the $i$th coordinate is a local generator.

source.place: Tag 0BXR (birational normalization); elementary generic-germ injection and standard projective-coordinate charts

proof.text: Choose coordinates on $V$ so that the last $r-s$ basis vectors span the restriction kernel and the first $s$ restrict to a basis. Then $Y$ lies scheme-theoretically in the linear subspace cut out by the last $r-s$ coordinates, namely $\mathbf P^{s-1}$; the original closed immersion factors as a closed immersion into this subspace. Indeed, on each standard affine chart its defining ideal contains those linear equations. No smaller linear subspace contains $Y$, by independence of the first $s$ restrictions. Also $s\ne0$, since the coordinates generate the nonzero invertible sheaf. If $s=1$, on the unique generating-section chart every coordinate ratio is constant, and the embedding factors through a single $k$-point. A dimension-one closed subscheme cannot be a closed subscheme of $\operatorname{Spec}k$ (its ideals are only $0,k$). Thus $s\ge2$. The map $C\to Y\to\mathbf P^{s-1}$ is the coordinate morphism of the generating space $U$, as in [def-weil-pbc-morphism-to-projective-space-by-sections].

source.place: Proof (3), stable-curve/GIT prerequisite: elementary coordinate description of the linear span

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-curve-section-degree-cap] with $A=L$, $m=1$, $q=0$ and the zero divisor $B$. The number $n=h^0(C,L)$ is finite and satisfies $n\le e+1$, since $e>0$. The inclusion of $U$ gives $s\le n\le e+1$. Suppose henceforth $s=e+1$. These inequalities force $U=H^0(C,L)$ and $n=e+1$.

source.place: Tag 0CCS (linear-series degree/dimension inequality); use only the inequality, not its unrestricted equality sentence

proof.text: Write $g=h^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$. Riemann--Roch [lem-sc-riemann-roch](1) gives $\chi(C,M)=\deg_{\rm div}M+1-g$ for every line bundle $M$, and $\chi(C,\mathcal O_C)=1-g$. Subtraction identifies the divisor degree with the Euler-characteristic degree used here. If $g=1$, the positive integer $e$ satisfies $e\ge2g-1$; [lem-sc-riemann-roch-large-degree] gives $n=e$, contradicting $n=e+1$. If $g\ge2$, apply [lem-sfb-linear-series-degree-dimension-bound] to $C,L,U$. Its degree $a$ satisfies $0\le a\le e$ and $s\le\max\{a+1-g,a/2+1\}$. But $a+1-g\le e-1<e+1$ and $a/2+1\le e/2+1<e+1$, again a contradiction. Since genus is a nonnegative integer, $g=0$.

source.place: Tag 0BS6 (Riemann--Roch); numerical genus-one and genus-at-least-two cases using the existing linear-series node

proof.text: Apply the genus-zero clause of [lem-sfb-low-genus-pointed-automorphism-rigidity] with automorphism $\operatorname{id}_C$: it gives $C\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$. Moreover $e\ge1=2g+1$, so [lem-sc-degree-2g1-very-ample] makes $L$ very ample. By [def-sc-ample], its complete linear system is a closed immersion into $\mathbf P(H^0(C,L)^\vee)$. Since $U=H^0(C,L)$, the coordinate map of step 3 is exactly this complete-system map after choosing its basis. Thus $C\xrightarrow\nu Y\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^{s-1}$ is a closed immersion.

proof.text:
The preceding composite being a closed immersion forces $
u$ to be an isomorphism here. Explicitly, on an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}R$ of the span meeting $Y$, write $Y\cap\operatorname{Spec}R=\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)$ and $C\cap\operatorname{Spec}R=\operatorname{Spec}(R/J)$. These presentations exist because both maps to the span are closed immersions [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Factorization gives $I\subseteq J$. The surjectivity of $
u$ from step 1 gives $\sqrt I=\sqrt J$ (the closed subsets coincide). Since $Y$ is integral, $I$ is prime. Thus $I\subseteq J\subseteq\sqrt J=I$, so $I=J$. These local isomorphisms glue to the given map $
u$. Hence $Y\simeq C\simeq\mathbf P^1$.

source.place: Tag 0BXR and the affine quotient description of a closed immersion; elementary prime-ideal calculation

proof.text: On $C\simeq\mathbf P^1$, [lem-sc-line-bundle-rational-section] writes $L\simeq\mathcal O(D)$ for a finite divisor $D$. By [def-sc-pic0] and the degree agreement in step 5, $\deg D=e$. Use the coordinates of [def-sc-p1-standard], with $\infty=\mathbf P^1\setminus\operatorname{Spec}k[t]$. Every other closed point is $t=a$ for $a\in k$, since $k$ is algebraically closed. At $a$ the element $t-a$ has order one, at infinity it is $s^{-1}(1-as)$ and has order minus one, and it is a unit at other points. Thus, by [def-sc-divisor], $\operatorname{div}(t-a)=[a]-[\infty]$. If $D=\sum_a n_a[a]+n_\infty[\infty]$, the finite product $f=\prod_a(t-a)^{n_a}$ has $\operatorname{div}(f)=D-e[\infty]$. Therefore [lem-sc-divisor-class-curve] identifies $\mathcal O(D)$ with $\mathcal O(e[\infty])$. The latter is $\mathcal O(e)$: its generator on $U_0$ is $1$ and on $U_1$ is $s^{-e}$, related by $1=t^{-e}s^{-e}$, precisely [def-sc-p1-standard]. Consequently the embedding of $Y$ in its span is the complete system $|\mathcal O(e)|$.

source.place: Tag 0BE9 (divisor classes and invertible modules); explicit two-chart divisor computation on the projective line

proof.text: Conversely, suppose $Y\simeq\mathbf P^1$ and its embedding in its span is the complete system $|\mathcal O(e)|$. Its defining coordinate space therefore has dimension $h^0(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O(e))=e+1$ by [lem-sc-p1-monomial](i), where $e>0$ was already proved. Restriction of ambient linear forms onto the linear span is surjective (extend any linear form from a vector subspace to a basis of the ambient vector space), so this dimension is exactly the original $s$. This proves the converse. Finally, if $Y$ is not such a rational normal curve, equality $s=e+1$ is excluded; the integer inequality $s\le e+1$ then gives $s\le e$.
